children: Poland’s draft budget for 2027 does not outline measures to consolidate public finances and the risk of public debt exceeding 55% of gross domestic product is very high, according to an opinion published by the Fiscal Council on Monday.
"The (55% of GDP) threshold is exceeded in almost all the risk scenarios analyzed ... The project therefore fails to provide an adequate safety margin," the Fiscal Council said.
"Although the constitutional threshold of 60% of GDP will not be exceeded in 2027, the council assesses the risk of breaching it as high for 2028 and very high for the years 2029-2030."

The Finance Ministry said in a statement that according to Polish law the Fiscal Council's opinion should pertain only to 2027 and that its comments on public debt further into the future were based on "arbitrary assumptions... that lack a basis in either EU or Polish law".
Under Polish law, breaching the 55% and 60% threshholds according to domestic methodology would mean the government has to implement austerity measures.

Poland expects its general government deficit to remain unchanged at 7.1% of GDP in 2027, the same level now planned for this year, fuelled by record deliveries of military equipment. The budget deficit for 2027 is expected to be 286.6 billion zlotys ($76.57 billion).

The government has argued that the high deficit is the result of record defence spending, which is set to reach 198 billion zlotys, or more than 4.5% of GDP, next year. In total, next year's budget expenditures are projected to amount to 977.6 billion zlotys.
According to the Fiscal Council, defence spending is not the only reason behind the deterioration of public finances.
"It accounts for approximately one-quarter of the increase in expenditure since 2021; social transfers, wages, and other permanent state obligations also play a significant role," it said.

The council also said that the budget expenditure forecast is subject to high risk, among other things, due to the inclusion of changes in the tax system that have not yet been adopted by Parliament, adding that tax revenues are "optimistic."
The Fiscal Council is an independent fiscal watchdog that assesses the government's budget plans, macroeconomic forecasts and compliance with domestic and European Union fiscal rules.
It does not have the power to veto the budget or government decisions, but its opinions carry weight and the Finance Ministry must respond to its observations.
